controls.statement: AI-assisted work begins with intent that a human can explain and review.
Non-trivial changes consistently start from durable goals, constraints, non-goals, edge cases, and acceptance criteria.
Decision rationale and definitions of done are shared standards and incomplete intent is rejected before implementation.
The organization detects and repairs intent debt across agent workflows using maintained evidence and ownership.
Developers deliberately provide project context when using coding agents.
A cold-start agent can discover project boundaries, architecture, commands, and verification paths from maintained artifacts.
Shared rules, skills, hooks, context bundles, and task memory have owners and are improved through review.
The harness and knowledge system demonstrably improve outcomes across repositories or teams.
Humans supervise AI suggestions and remain responsible for executed changes.
Bounded delegated workflows have explicit permissions, stop conditions, and human handback points.
Isolation, maker-checker separation, parallel execution, and review capacity are deliberately engineered.
Guarded autonomous loops routinely complete meaningful work within enforced blast-radius and duration limits.
A human reads and owns AI-assisted changes before they affect users.
Review depth follows risk and explicitly checks common AI-generated failure modes.
Evidence-gated intake and independent checking are standard for non-trivial or high-risk work.
Automated triage reliably routes low-risk work and escalates anomalous or expensive changes for human judgment.
AI-assisted changes are followed by relevant executable checks.
Required CI gates cover the relevant quality bar and cannot be silently bypassed.
The workflow detects weakened tests, removed thresholds, skipped checks, and behavior changed merely to satisfy generated output.
Critical paths use high-signal techniques such as mutation, property, differential, or equivalent adversarial testing.
Agents have explicit boundaries for sensitive data, credentials, production, and destructive actions.
Secrets, permissions, provenance, and production access are technically controlled rather than left to prompts alone.
Third-party tools are vetted, destructive actions are blocked, untrusted inputs are isolated, and exceptions are auditable.
Organization-wide audits and incident evidence show that guardrails work and improve over time.
Engineers are expected to understand and explain generated changes.
The team names and challenges unsafe surrender behaviors such as unread acceptance and specification-free implementation.
Load-bearing systems have explicit human ownership and role-specific AI literacy expectations.
The organization preserves time, authority, and incentives for engineering judgment as automated output grows.
Useful prompts or workflows are intentionally reused.
Shared instructions, templates, rules, or skills are versioned and discoverable.
Repeated failures become reviewed tests, hooks, rules, or checker behavior with named ownership.
Evaluated capabilities are shared across repositories or teams and retired when they stop adding value.
The team can identify where and how AI contributes to engineering work.
Adoption, cost, provenance, rework, and quality signals are visible enough to guide decisions.
Named owners review trends and AI-related incidents, then change the operating system in response.
Trend evidence shows fewer repeated failures and stable or improving quality as agent-driven volume increases.
